title: Queen against rook III: breaking the third-rank defence
summary: The rook's barrier on the third and fourth ranks, the quiet move that breaks it, the diagonal motif and the stalemate traps.
part.third.title: The rook on the third
part.third.summary: The rook blocks our king's way. A quiet queen move leaves it without a square.
part.best.title: The best defence
part.best.summary: When the black king leaves the edge, the queen crosses to the other side with checks and the rook leaves the third rank.
part.edge.title: The rook on the edge
part.edge.summary: With the rook on a6, our king walks round and attacks it from below.
part.fourth.title: The fourth rank
part.fourth.summary: A check pushes the black king back, a quiet move keeps it there, and our king walks round the rook.
part.diagonal.title: The diagonal motif
part.diagonal.summary: The rook on our king's diagonal threatens checks from two sides. The queen goes to the square that covers both.
part.behind.title: Queen first
part.behind.summary: For the king to approach without giving the rook checks, the queen steps onto its line first.
part.stalemate.title: The stalemates
part.stalemate.summary: With the black king out of squares, the rook offers itself, with check or without. That is how Morozevich let the win slip.
part.map.title: Browne vs the computer
part.map.summary: Browne's rematch against the computer, the stages of the ending and the practical challenge.
step.t_third: This is the most stubborn defence of the ending. The black king is on the edge and the rook, on its third rank, on b6, blocks our king's way. As long as the rook has a safe square on that rank there is no progress, and checks do not help. Which queen move leaves the rook without a safe square on its rank?
step.t_third.hint1: Count the squares on the rook's rank that our king and queen watch now. Which ones are left for it?
step.t_third.hint2: From another square the queen would watch both ends of the rank at once, even if it looks like a retreat.
step.barrier: Look at the rook's rank. Our king watches c6, d6 and e6; the queen watches e6, f6 and g6. That leaves a6, b6 and h6, and the rook is comfortable. Checking does not help, because the black king just walks from side to side behind the rook. John Nunn writes that a strong player can break the second-rank defence by calculation, but this one has to be known in advance. What breaks it is a quiet move that looks like a retreat.
step.d_fork: The idea is 1.Qf4, a quiet move. See what happens if the rook tries to stay on the rank by going to g6.
step.d_fork.m1: 1.Qf4! From f4 the queen eyes b8, f8 and h6. Now c6, d6 and e6 belong to the king, f6 and h6 to the queen, and the ends a6 and g6 fall to a fork.
step.d_fork.m2: 1...Rg6. The rook tries the end on the queen's side, far from our king.
step.d_fork.m3: 2.Qf8+. First a check along the back rank, which drives the black king off d8 and prepares the fork.
step.d_fork.m4: 2...Kd7. The king steps up to d7, the square that looks safest.
step.d_fork.m5: 3.Qf7+! From f7 the queen checks along the seventh rank and hits g6 along the diagonal at the same time. That is the fork.
step.d_fork.m6: 3...Kd8. The king has to get out of check, and the rook is left undefended.
step.d_fork.m7: 4.Qxg6. The rook is gone. That is why g6 was not a safe square, and a6, on the other side, falls the same way.
step.ra6: Now the other end: after 1.Qf4 Ra6, the rook went to the edge of the board. Same pattern on the other side: a check on the back rank and a fork.
step.ra6.hint: First the check on the back rank, on the rook's side. Then the square from which the queen checks and hits a6 at the same time.
step.ra6.done: 2.Qb8+ Ke7 3.Qb7+, and the rook falls. Both ends fall the same way because from f4 the queen was eyeing b8 and f8 at once.
step.t_best: This is the best defence: after 1.Qf4 Kd7, the black king left the edge instead of moving the rook, and the rook stays on b6, closing the rank. How does the queen cross to the other side of the board without losing time?
step.t_best.hint1: On the other side of the board, the queen gets close to the rook while giving check.
step.t_best.hint2: Each queen move has to be a check, so Black has no time to rearrange the rook.
step.switch: Nunn says this is the point of the technique: the queen switches sides with check, giving Black no time. From the a-file side, the queen gets close to the rook, and after one more check it will have to step in front of the king and leave the third rank.
step.d_switch: The queen switches sides with checks, and our king walks in.
step.d_switch.m1: 2.Qa4+! Check along the diagonal, on the rook's side. The black king has to move, and the queen is already on the other side.
step.d_switch.m2: 2...Kc7. The best escape: the king stays next to the rook and defends it.
step.d_switch.m3: 3.Qa7+. The queen comes right up to the rook with check. If the king runs to c8 or d8, the queen captures on b6.
step.d_switch.m4: 3...Rb7. The rook steps in front of the king and leaves the third rank. The barrier is down.
step.d_switch.m5: 4.Qc5+. Check along the c-file, which drives the black king away from the centre.
step.d_switch.m6: 4...Kb8. The king goes to the corner, next to the rook.
step.d_switch.m7: 5.Kd6. Our king has crossed the barrier. Queen and king close, the rook on the second rank: it is the defence from the last lesson.
step.home: Same line, one move on: after 5.Kd6 Rg7, the rook went looking for checks. Put the queen in the centre, and the rook comes back next to its king. Then the diagonal position appears, with the triangle you know.
step.home.hint: First the queen to the centre, on a square that takes the checks away from the rook. After 6...Rc7, the queen makes the triangle you know until the diagonal position.
step.home.done: The diagonal position, with After 9...Rb7, 10.Kc6+ is a discovered check and we reach Philidor. From the third rank to here took about ten moves.
step.t_thirdA: The rook is still on the third rank, but now on the edge, on a6. Nunn says it is enough to know two third-rank positions, and this is the second one. Do you really need a queen move, or can our king drive the rook away?
step.t_thirdA.hint1: A rook on the end of the rank can be attacked from below.
step.t_thirdA.hint2: The king walks round via the c-file; the queen only needs to keep the black king out of the way.
step.a6: Here the quiet queen move is not needed. On the edge the rook has a weakness: our king gets below it, via c5 and b5, and attacks it. The queen has just one job, to stop the black king coming over to defend the rook.
step.d_around: The king walks round, and the queen just keeps the black king out of the way.
step.d_around.m1: 1.Kc5. The king heads below the rook and threatens 2.Kb5, attacking a6. From c5 it already watches b6.
step.d_around.m2: 1...Kc8. The black king hurries to defend the rook via b7.
step.d_around.m3: 2.Qe7! A quiet move. The queen takes the seventh rank and d8, and the black king can only go to b8.
step.d_around.m4: 2...Kb8. From b8 the black king does not protect a6.
step.d_around.m5: 3.Kb5. The king attacks the rook. Staying on the third rank costs the rook, so Black takes it off.
step.d_around.m6: 3...Ra7. The rook goes to the seventh, glued to its king: the second-rank defence, which you already know how to break.
step.kc8: Back to the rook on b6. This time, after 1.Qf4 Kc8, the black king went to the other side. The rook will end up on the edge, and you use the same walk round with the king.
step.kc8.hint: 2.Kc5 attacks the rook. When it goes to the edge, keep the black king out of the way with the queen and walk round.
step.kc8.done: 2.Kc5 Ra6 3.Qe4 Kc7 4.Qe7+ Kb8 5.Kb5: this is Nunn's line, and the rook has to leave the third rank.
step.t_fourth: One step before the third rank: the rook cuts our king off along the fourth, and the black king is still far from the edge, on d7. How do you push the black king back and keep it there?
step.t_fourth.hint1: First a check that drives the black king off the seventh rank.
step.t_fourth.hint2: Then a quiet queen move that watches the squares it would come back through.
step.fourth: Nunn says the fourth rank is the easiest barrier to break: the defender ends up pushed back to the third or the second. The plan has three beats. A check pushes the black king back, a quiet move keeps it there, and our king walks round below the rook, heading for b4, to drive it off the rank.
step.d_fourth: Nunn's line, with the black king retreating.
step.d_fourth.m1: 1.Qf7+. Check along the seventh rank: the black king must retreat to the back rank or step up to the sixth.
step.d_fourth.m2: 1...Kd8. The king retreats to the edge. Stepping up to d6 leads to another, trickier line.
step.d_fourth.m3: 2.Qe6! The quiet move. The queen watches c8, d7, e7 and e8, and the black king only has c7.
step.d_fourth.m4: 2...Kc7. The only square. The black king will not get back to the centre.
step.d_fourth.m5: 3.Kd3. Our king walks round below, heading for c3 and b4.
step.d_fourth.m6: 3...Rc5. The rook cuts the c-file to slow the king down.
step.d_fourth.m7: 4.Kd4. The king attacks the rook, and it has to go. If 4...Rc1, 5.Qe3 pushes it back, and after 5...Rc6 the defence becomes the third-rank one, sideways.
step.m99: Now a real game: Morozevich against Jakovenko, Pamplona, 2006. Morozevich had a knight and pawns against the rook; Jakovenko captured the knight with 70...Rxd4, but Morozevich queened with 71.g8=Q, and queen against rook lasted more than forty moves. On move 99, the rook on h4 cuts our king off along the fourth rank and the black king is on f2. Play like Morozevich: lock the black king in and undo the barrier.
step.m99.hint: A quiet queen move that takes the whole third rank away from the black king.
step.m99.done: 99.Qd3! David Smerdon, who annotated the game, writes that here the fourth-rank defence is broken. After 99...Rh7 100.Qd4+ Kf3, 101.Kg5! the king advances without a check: the moves that make the most progress are often not checks. Notice 99...Rh7: the rook went to the diagonal of our king, which was on f5. That is the subject of the next chapter.
step.t_diag: In the fourth-rank line, our king went to d4 instead of d3, and after 3.Kd4 Ra1, the rook ran to a1, on the same diagonal as the king. Which checks does it threaten now, and from which square does the queen take both away at once?
step.t_diag.hint1: The rook threatens one check down the d-file and another along the fourth rank.
step.t_diag.hint2: There is a square from which the queen watches d1 and a4 at the same time.
step.diag: This is the diagonal motif, and it turns up in master games. In Morozevich against Jakovenko, our king was on e6 and Jakovenko played 79...Rg8!, putting the rook on the white king's diagonal. From there it threatens checks from two sides, and the queen cannot find a check that hits king and rook together. Nunn teaches that the motif works well when the rook is at least three squares from the king. Here it was only two away, and in the next chapter you will see how Morozevich could have taken advantage.
step.d_diag: In the position after 3.Kd4 Ra1, the answer is to put the queen on the square that covers both checks.
step.d_diag.m1: 4.Qb3! From b3 the queen watches d1 and a4, the two squares the rook would check from. The diagonal motif has lost its bite.
step.d_diag.m2: 4...Kd6. The black king steps up towards the centre.
step.d_diag.m3: 5.Qb4+. Check along the diagonal, pushing the black king away from the rook.
step.d_diag.m4: 5...Ke6. The king retreats, and the rook is still alone on a1.
step.d_diag.m5: 6.Kc5. Our king advances. The rule to take away: before moving the king, see which square on its diagonal the rook can reach, and whether the queen watches the two checks it would give from there. If not, pick another square for the king.
step.d_short: Now the short motif, in a position built from Nunn's analysis. The rook on a2 is on our king's diagonal, but only two squares away, and Nunn says the motif only works well at three squares or more. See why.
step.d_short.m1: 1.Qf6! A quiet move: the queen steps back to check from afar, along the seventh rank and the diagonal. The rook's checks are no worry: after 1...Ra4+, 2.Kb5 already attacks it.
step.d_short.m2: 1...Ra6. The rook goes back to its third rank, next to the king, which protects it.
step.d_short.m3: 2.Qd4+. Check along the diagonal: the black king has to leave a7.
step.d_short.m4: 2...Kb8. The most stubborn defence: the king runs to the back rank, away from our king, and leaves the rook on a6 unprotected.
step.shortB: The rook on a6 was left unprotected after 2...Kb8, and the short motif threatens nothing. It is our king's turn.
step.shortB.hint: With the rook two squares away, the king does not need to wait for the queen: go straight at it.
step.shortB.done: 3.Kb5! Our king attacks the rook, and its best way out is 3...Ra7, glued to the black king: the second-rank defence. That completes the rule: with the rook three or more squares from our king, the queen covers both checks before the king moves; with the rook two squares away, the motif is short, and the king can go ahead, because it stays close to the rook and attacks it.
step.t_behind: Morozevich against Jakovenko again, move 81. Our king wants to get close to the black king, but every step it takes can hand the rook a string of checks. Which move improves the position without giving the rook a single check?
step.t_behind.hint1: See from which squares the rook would check the white king after each of its steps.
step.t_behind.hint2: Look for the king step after which the checking squares are already watched, by the queen or by the king itself.
step.behind: Morozevich played 81.Qc3+ Kb5 82.Kd6, and the rook checked with 82...Rg6+ and, after 83.Kc7, moved away with 83...Rg4!!, one of the most stubborn defences, according to Smerdon. He points to 81.Ke7! as much better. With the king on e7 the rook has no check: on g7 it would be captured by the queen, which watches the diagonal from d4 to g7, and on e8 it would be captured by the king. The rule: queen before king.
step.d_behind: In a constructed position, the same idea: the queen steps behind the king before it moves.
step.d_behind.m1: 1.Qf3! The queen goes to our king's file, right behind it. When the king leaves the f-file, the queen will give a discovered check to the black king on f6.
step.d_behind.m2: 1...Rh7. The rook waits for our king to step so it can start checking.
step.d_behind.m3: 2.Kg4+! The king leaves the f-file and the queen gives a discovered check. Black has to deal with the king, and the rook gets no time for its checks.
step.d_behind.m4: 2...Kg6. The black king gets out of check.
step.d_behind.m5: 3.Qe4+. Another check along the diagonal, pushing the black king to the edge.
step.d_behind.m6: 3...Kh6. The black king is on the h-file, and our king can come close.
step.behindB: The black king is on the edge, after 3.Qe4+ Kh6. Bring our king one step closer.
step.behindB.hint: The square near the black king where a rook check leads nowhere.
step.behindB.done: 4.Kf5! The king is close. If the rook checks on f7, 5.Ke6 attacks it, and it has to run again.
step.t_ponziani: Queen and king close, the black king trapped on the edge, and Even so, this position is a draw. What can the rook do, and which of our pieces is badly placed?
step.t_ponziani.hint2: After each capture of the rook, count the black king's squares. Is any left?
step.ponziani: This position is Ponziani's, from 1782. With 1...Rg7+! the rook starts checking from f7, g7 and h7. Our king cannot run to the e-file, because the rook would pin the queen; and if it captures the rook, as in 2.Kf6 Rg6+ 3.Kxg6, the black king is stalemated. The flaw is the queen on e6, glued to the black king: with it there, the rook can offer itself.
step.d_desperado: Morozevich against Jakovenko, the end of the game, after 110.Qg3+ Kh1. Smerdon calls the check natural but not part of the plan; the game could still be won with the queen far away. See what happened.
step.d_desperado.m1: 111.Kf3?? Morozevich brings the king closer. Smerdon calls this the decisive mistake: the queen on g3 and the king on f3 take every square from the black king.
step.d_desperado.m2: 111...Rf2+!! The rook offers itself with check. If 112.Kxf2 or 112.Qxf2, the black king is stalemated.
step.d_desperado.m3: 112.Ke3. The king runs from the check, but the rook follows it.
step.d_desperado.m4: 112...Re2+. Another check, and the rook keeps offering itself.
step.d_desperado.m5: 113.Kd3. The king keeps running along the third rank.
step.d_desperado.m6: 113...Rd2+. The rook will not leave the king alone.
step.d_desperado.m7: 114.Kxd2. Morozevich captured, and the black king was stalemated. A draw, after more than forty moves a queen up.
step.moro: Go back to move 110 and win the game Morozevich did not win. The queen had to stay far away, in the centre, and the king come closer afterwards, without letting the rook sacrifice itself.
step.moro.hint: Start with 110.Qe5, far from the black king, and only then bring our king in.
step.moro.done: 110.Qe5! Kg1 111.Kg3! Rg2+ 112.Kh3!, Smerdon's line. The rook is attacked and has no way to sacrifice itself: the queen, from a distance, leaves the black king a square. Queen far, king close.
step.loose: Now a constructed position in which the rook offers itself without check. Before capturing, count the black king's squares.
step.loose.hint: After 1.Qxg3, where would the black king go?
step.loose.done: 1.Qxg3? would be stalemate: the king on a8 would have neither a7, b7 nor b8. With 1.Qa1+ Kb8 2.Qh8+, the rook has to block on g8 and falls with mate.
step.t_browne: One of the worst positions of the ending: our king is far from the black king and the loose rook can check from everywhere. What is the plan, stage by stage, until the rook is captured?
step.t_browne.hint1: Remember what you learned, from the end backwards: Philidor, the second rank, the third, the fourth.
step.t_browne.hint2: Of the stages you learned, which comes first with the pieces far apart? Start by bringing the king in without walking into checks.
step.map: This is the position from Walter Browne's rematch against the computer Belle, on 30 December 1978. Browne played from home, over the phone, and had fifty moves to capture the rook; with perfect play 31 are enough. He found 15.Qd1!, which he said deserved an exclamation mark, but between moves 16 and 21 he made no progress. That was the third- and fourth-rank barrier, where Ken Thompson, the program's author, had seen weaker players go wrong. Browne fought it, crossed it, and on the last move captured the rook with 50.Qxa1. The road is the one from this lesson: bring the king, undo the fourth and third ranks, go through the second and reach Philidor.
step.recap: Three rules to take from this lesson. One: against the third rank, a quiet queen move that looks like a retreat takes every square on the rank from the rook. Two: before moving the king, look at its diagonal and at the rook's checks; the queen gets there first, covering those checks. Three: in the corner, queen far away; if the rook offers itself, with check or without, count the black king's squares before capturing.
step.finish: Your turn in the practical challenge, from the third rank. Break the barrier, go through the second rank, reach Philidor and capture the rook.
practice: The position from Browne's rematch, one of the worst in the ending: with perfect play it takes 31 moves to capture the rook, and you have fifty. Bring the king, take the checks away, break the barriers one by one and reach Philidor.
ex.e12: The black king is stuck on the back rank, and the rook on h7 is loose, right in front of the queen. Win without falling into the trap.
ex.e12.hint: Before capturing, look at the black king's squares: our king already watches e7 and e8.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qf4+! After 1...Rf7, 2.Qe5 takes g7 from the black king, and the win goes on. 1.Qxh7? would be stalemate: the king on f8 would have neither e7 nor e8, watched by our king, nor f7, g7 and g8, watched by the queen on h7. That is exactly why the rook offered itself for free, without check. Other queen moves also win, but more slowly; the check down the f-file is the only move that does not delay the win.
ex.e18: Morozevich against Jakovenko, Pamplona 2006, move 93. The rook on a4 cuts our king off along the fourth rank and the black king roams the third. Lock the black king behind the barrier.
ex.e18.hint: It is the start of the lesson's fourth rank, sideways: a check that pushes the black king back one rank and a quiet move that keeps it there.
ex.e18.solution: 93.Qf1+ and, after 93...Kd2, 94.Qf3. The queen on the third rank takes c3, d3 and e3 from the black king: it is stuck on the first and second ranks, and the rook, alone on the fourth, starts to lose its support. They are the only moves that do not delay the win. In the game Morozevich played 93.Qd6+ and let the black king back to the centre via e3: the win moved eight moves further away.
ex.e19: Our king wants to walk down to the black king, but the rook on b4 cuts off the fourth rank and waits for its first step to start checking. Prepare the king's march.
ex.e19.hint: If our king leaves the f-file, which piece could give check to the black king along it?
ex.e19.solution: 1.Qf7! The queen steps back behind our king, on the f-file, the black king's file. Now every king step off the file is a discovered check. After 1...Rb2, 2.Ke4+ Ke1 3.Qc4 Kd2 4.Kd4, and the king has reached the centre, where the rook has no check; on move 2, 2.Qc4 is just as good. If 1...Rb5+, 2.Kg4+! is a discovered check, and the win comes even faster. Beware of 1.Qg4??, which seems to shut the fourth rank: 1...Rxg4 2.Kxg4 is a draw. Queen checks such as 1.Qh2+ win, but much more slowly.
ex.e14: The rook is on the f-file, two files from the black king, and our king is far away. Set up the attack and, once the barrier is up, break it.
ex.e14.hint: Turn the board sideways: it is the lesson's third rank. Bring the king in front of the black king and remember which queen move left the rook without a square.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Ke4, hitting the rook; 2.Qg3, which keeps the black king on the h-file; 3.Ke5, the only move that does not push the win further away; and, with the rook on f7, 4.Qd3. It is the lesson position turned sideways: here 4.Qd3 plays the role of the lesson's quiet move to f4, and the rook has no safe square on the f-file. 4.Qb3 and 4.Qc3 do the same.
ex.e15: The rook on f4 is on our king's diagonal, three squares away, and threatens checks from two sides. Disarm the rook.
ex.e15.hint: First find the two squares from which the rook would check our king. The queen does not need to give check: it only has to watch both.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Qg8! From g8 the queen watches f7, right next to it, and, along the diagonal, c4: the two squares the rook would check from. If 1...Rf7+ or 1...Rc4+, the queen captures the rook. Queen checks such as 1.Qd6+ push the win much further away: after 1...Kg5 the black king gets off the edge. After 1...Rf6, 2.Qg4 watches g5, g6, g7 and h5, and the black king is stuck on the h-file.
ex.e16: The fourth rank again, but the black king stepped up to d6 instead of going back. Nunn calls the third move of this line the trickiest moment. Find all three.
ex.e16.hint: The queen has to take a4 away from the rook. Then pick the king square where, if the rook goes to its diagonal, the queen still arrives in time to watch both checks.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qe8, the only move that keeps the pace: the queen covers a4. After 1...Kc7, 2.Qe6, and the rook goes to b5. Now 3.Kd4! If the rook goes to the diagonal with 3...Rb2, it is two squares from the king, the lesson's short motif: it threatens checks on d2 and b4, and the queen reaches a5, which watches both squares, with checks: 4.Qe5+ Kd7 5.Qf5+ Kd6 6.Qa5. With 3.Kd3? the rook goes to b1 and threatens 4...Rd1+. The queen on e6 already watches b3, but cannot reach in one move any square that watches d1 and b3 at once; it needs quiet moves, and the win gets five moves further away. Nunn's line (2002): 1.Qe8 and 3.Kd4 are the only moves that do not delay the win.
key.third: The third-rank barrier: the rook blocks the white king's path. A quiet queen move, without check, leaves the rook with no good square.
key.thirdA: The same barrier with the rook on the edge of the board: here the white king walks round behind it and drives it away.
key.fourth: The rook builds its barrier one rank further out. It falls apart the same way: the queen pushes the black king back with checks and the white king goes round the rook.
key.ponziani: Ponziani, 1782: queen and king have come too close. The rook gives check after check, and if the white king captures it, the black king is stalemated. A draw.
key.browne: The position from Browne's rematch against the computer in 1978: the pieces start far apart, and the road to winning the rook is a long one.
history: Queen against rook has a stage that hardly anyone knew how to play: the rook settles on a rank close to its king and blocks the enemy king's way through. As early as 1895 a whole book on this ending appeared in London, signed by a mysterious Euclid, and still the textbooks did not explain how to get past that barrier. When Walter Browne took on the computer in 1978, that was where he struggled most before getting through. Grandmaster John Nunn wrote that a strong player can break the second-rank defence at the board, but this defence has to be known in advance. It still decides games today: in 2006, in Pamplona, Morozevich got through it against Jakovenko with a few inaccuracies and then, close to victory, let the game end in stalemate.
